lesson.title: Tcpdump: Packet Capture Without a Screen
lesson.summary: Tcpdump is a command-line packet capture tool built on the same underlying capture engine as Wireshark, built for the reality that most servers you need to troubleshoot only give you a terminal.
lesson.body:
Wireshark assumes you have a graphical desktop in front of you. Most of the servers that actually need network troubleshooting, cloud instances, data center machines, embedded devices, do not offer one. You reach them over SSH, and SSH gives you a terminal, not a window manager. Tcpdump exists for exactly this situation: it captures and displays packets as text, directly in the terminal, with no graphical dependency at all.

Underneath, tcpdump and Wireshark are close relatives. Both rely on the same operating system capture facilities to pull packets off a network interface, and both understand the same layered packet structure built from the packet concept and application-layer protocols like DNS and HTTP. The real difference is the interface: tcpdump prints one compact line per packet to standard output, using a filter syntax (Berkeley Packet Filter expressions) to narrow down which packets you see. That makes it fast to run interactively, easy to script, and light enough to leave running briefly on a production server without much overhead.

A simple example: you suspect a server is not receiving DNS responses correctly. Running tcpdump -i eth0 -n port 53 shows every DNS query and response crossing that interface in real time, with -n telling tcpdump not to resolve hostnames itself, which would be slow and would also add the very DNS traffic you are trying to observe. If you need to look more closely later, or hand the capture to a colleague, you can write it to disk instead of printing it: tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap host 10.0.0.5 and port 443 records only the TLS traffic to and from a specific host into a pcap file. That file opens directly in Wireshark, which is the normal division of labor in practice: tcpdump for capturing on a remote or headless machine where you only have a shell, Wireshark afterward for the deeper visual inspection with filters, colorization, and stream reconstruction.

A second example shows why the filter expression matters. Suppose connections to a backend service keep dropping unexpectedly. Rather than capturing everything, which on a busy server can produce an unmanageable volume of traffic, you can target exactly the behavior you are chasing: tcpdump -i any -n 'tcp port 8080 and (tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0)' captures only packets carrying a TCP RST flag on port 8080, the packets that actually tear connections down. Filtering at capture time, rather than capturing everything and searching afterward, is one of the most useful habits tcpdump teaches, and it works because BPF filters are applied efficiently before the packet is even fully copied out of the kernel.
